review_text_raw:
This game has everything I love. The operator is enjoyable from start to finish, and the story is an absolute banger. I was surprised to find voice acting, which I wasn’t expecting, but it added a lot to the experience. The characters are engaging, and I genuinely enjoyed speaking with them. The choices you can make during calls felt natural—definitely things I would have actually said, which was great.

The gameplay itself is pretty self-explanatory while still having some depth. Even though it’s mostly clicking and a bit of typing, it still managed to pull me in with the story. I felt a real sense of accomplishment whenever I solved something. At first, the story was incredibly gripping—I had no idea what was going on and was eager to piece it together. However, as it progressed towards the final parts, it became much easier to predict, and I had already figured things out before the game revealed them.

I was able to complete every achievement in a single playthrough, which took about 3-4 hours. If you enjoy mystery and crime investigation, you’ll probably love this.

Overall, I’d definitely recommend it to anyone, but maybe wait for a sale, as it could be considered pricey given its short length and relatively simple gameplay.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

I grade The Operator A-. This is an excellent investigation game with a great premise and fantastic presentation, including the music. While it doesn't have Hollywood-style hacking, given that its setting is in 1992 and you're working in a government alphabet agency, the developers nailed the look and feel of a stripped down government UI. Even right down to a part where you use an even [i]older[/i] computer and the visual area changes from 16:9 to 4:3. Nice touch.

The story is very well written. I didn't detect a single typo or weird turn of phrase. A lot of detective games here on Steam are made by non-English developers, and so they tend to get wonky in localization. The Operator does not have that issue. The story is almost entirely logical and internally consistent, and it was fun to experience.

The only thing is the story's wheels fell off at the very end. While the story beats and twists were a bit obvious, the final hard twist -- though it was presented really well -- makes absolutely no logical sense even within the context of the world that is presented to us. I come away from it with a lot more questions, but not the good "What are they going to do next?" kind. It's more the "Why did the basic premise happen in the first place?" kind. Unless there was some subtlety I missed, I can think of a thousand reasons why the first step of the plot shouldn't have happened, and that sort of makes the ending a little bit of a letdown.

But don't let that dissuade you. I'm happy to have bought the game and supported the developer, especially because the gameplay was excellent. I really enjoyed the act of investigating as a government agent and having tools like face-scanning and an omni-database just a mouse click away. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy games with hacking -- whether Hollwood hacking like Orwell or more script-based hacking like HackNet -- but it was really fun to be an agent for the "other side" and just have some improbable tools at my fingertips. If there is a sequel, while I hope the writing makes a little more logical sense, I really encourage the devs to keep the gameplay just as it is.

The Operator — Quick Review

Platform: PC (Steam)

Genre: Puzzle / Simulation / Mystery

Verdict: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A standout puzzle experience

---

What It Is

The Operator puts you in the role of a remote operator—essentially a digital detective working through cases from behind a screen. You dig through databases, analyze evidence, make phone calls, and piece together mysteries using a realistic desktop interface. It's the kind of game that makes you feel like you're actually doing the job.

Why It Works

The puzzle design is the star. The game doesn't hold your hand. You're given tools, a case file, and just enough rope to figure things out yourself. The satisfaction of connecting two pieces of evidence you found hours apart is genuinely rewarding. It respects your intelligence in a way few puzzle games do.

The interface feels authentic. The fake desktop OS, the clunky database searches, the phone calls—it all adds to the immersion. You're not just solving puzzles; you're inhabiting a role.

The layered structure keeps it fresh. Each case builds on what you've learned, but introduces new mechanics or twists so it never feels repetitive. By the time you've played "a couple layers" (as you put it), the game has opened up into something much deeper than it first appears.

The Vibe

It's methodical. Deliberate. If you want fast-paced action, this isn't it. But if you enjoy the slow burn of untangling a mystery—cross-referencing names, verifying alibis, catching contradictions—The Operator is incredibly satisfying.

Bottom Line

One of the better puzzle experiences on Steam right now. It trusts the player, delivers great "aha!" moments, and wraps it in a polished, believable package. Highly recommended if you enjoy games like Papers, Please, Orwell, or Return of the Obra Dinn.

Insanely good. In something of a trend started last week by my playthrough of Anger Foot, "this could have been an email, but you wrote an essay, and an excellent one at that". In other words: What could have been a simple gimmick indie that's fun and gone in one hour is turned upside down by excellent production value, which includes: great direction, engaging narrative, amazing atmosphere and voice acting. I couldn't believe how much stuff *goes on* in this game and by the end it felt like taking part in a conspiration-themed deep state thriller and not playing a puzzle solver, and that's despite spending most of the time (*most*) staring at computer screens.

I guess my only complaint is that the story is *only* good and you can see some twists coming from a mile away, but it more than makes up for that with excellent characters and being, well, engaging on a surprising level. The Operator is also not as open-ended as it seems to be, and could use a few more notable decisions or alternate endings.

Give this a go, there's much more to this title than meets the eye. Heck, if nothing else comes up this can be my personal GOTY.

review_text_raw:
I recommend it ... but with some qualifications. 

So, the presentation is excellent. Really builds a strong atmosphere of mystery. There are points when you really feel like you're an operator for a field agent uncovering a major conspiracy. The game does a very good job of doing that. Some of the puzzles took some thinking. They're not super-difficult, but they all make sense in the context of the game and there's not a lot of handholding. Overall, I like how it's all presented.

However ... what I didn't realize is that this is more visual novel than a true puzzle game. It's not a pure visual novel - there is some genuine gameplay here. And that gameplay is pretty good. But ultimately, the gameplay is to trigger the next scene. You can't really "fail" - or at least, you can't fail in a way that will affect the story.

I had believed the game to be a puzzler in the vein of Obra Dinn or Orwell. And I would say the gameplay is as good in part. But after a while, I could "see the rails" - see that at its core, it's a visual novel.

However, that's not why I was disappointed.

The bigger problem I had with the game is that I felt it was ... too short. Not in terms of game length - but in terms of the plot. It felt like it ended right when the plot was getting interesting. 

Putting spoilers on anything further:
[spoiler]Where the game ends, when the intrigue is getting intense and the identity twist is revealed ... I felt almost like that's where the real story is starting. 

Up until this point, our protagonist has just been faceless tech guy who doesn't have a role in the story - and suddenly now we understand how he ties into the conspiracy. And we also understand just what kind of terrible enemy we're up against. 

With this dramatic twist, we now understand the protagonist and his role in the story - as well as true nature and threat of the antagonist that he faces. The stakes have been made clear. The die is cast, the point of no return is reached. 

The question is, what happens now? What does our protagonist do with his new forbidden knowledge? And how can he defeat this terrible enemy?... but instead - the story unceremoniously ends right there. Not only is it kind of a bummer of an ending - but it feels like you stopped telling me this story exactly at the point where it became interesting. Right at the point where things had fully shifted from "Government Bureau Employee Simulator" to "Global Spy Conspiracy Thriller". Our agency has revealed they're evil and they betrayed us, we're gonna go rogue, and take the conspiracy down .... no, wait, actually, that's the end. [/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]It'd be like if moments after Jason Bourne realized that he was a secret agent and that assassins were trying to kill him ... he just died and the movie ended.

Or, to use a videogame equivalent - it'd be like if right when it's revealed that Doki Doki Literature Club is not actually an anime dating sim ... the game just ended.

There's no resolution. The story feels incomplete. If anything, this feels like it should be the prologue to the real plot. Like a teaser that gives us a glimpse of "OMG these guys are really bad". 

Actually, at the end, when it shifts to HAL's perspective - I thought that was where the real game was about to begin. like, "Twist, Tanner dies in the prologue! You're actually playing as HAL. How will HAL defeat the Organization?" ... But then the credits rolled.[/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]Part of the problem was that I figured out the twist long before it was revealed. I wasn't being clever, either - it was clear from the opening cutscene that we were not playing as some anonymous rando. We are obviously someone who is involved with this conspiracy in some way. As events played out, the only possibilities were either (a) you were secretly one of the missing people or (b) you were secretly the Ghost. When it became clear you weren't the Ghost ... well, there's only one missing person who we know by name, so that must be you.[/spoiler] 
 
I will say I was thoroughly engaged up until the ending. Even when it started to become clear that the story was more on rails that I'd hoped - I didn't mind because the presentation was so good and the story had me hooked. 

But when it ended ... I felt very disappointed because I was like, "Wait, we're ending it here? That's it?"

So I guess that's my recommend. It's a very well-done experience and the devs clearly were doing something right to keep me gripped. I intended to just try the game for a bit and ended up finishing it in one setting. But it really surprised me that it ended where it did.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Short and fun little deep state conspiracy game [/h1] 

First of all, this game is short.[b] VERY SHORT [/b]. It takes about 3-4 hours to complete, but the game tells the story it wants to tell in that time so it´s fine. 

[h3] Story 7/10 [/h3] 
The story is fine. It starts of strong, leaving you as the operator to figure out what you are doing and why you are doing it.
As soon as the story picks up the pace, the game is beginning to get more and more predictable. Sure, it makes sure to tell the story in a convincing way, but if the player has had any contact with books that follow similar plotlines or watched a few "rogue agent fighting conspiracy" movies you know where the plot is going and how the game will end. Ending was fine, a bit disappointing because the cut was fast and hard and resulted in a cliff hanger. To me it feels like the devs wrote a story thats about 10 hours long and just cut the game in half when they had the opportunity to do so, preparing the player for a future sequel.

[b] STORY SPOILERS [/b]
[spoiler] In my opinion the reveal that Mike Trench, our friend and FDI director, is the mole and head of the "Operator Program" was very predictable about half-way through  the game (ever since the Biolab incident and the player operator talking about "baiting out the mole"). The Ghost was written in a very stereotypical bad guy hitman way: I dont have a name, my identity was erased. I know the truth but can not tell you. You can ask any question as long as it is not "out of bounds". Yeah, very corny and kinda cringy. In general, even though the way it is written is good and convincing for the most part, sometimes the game feels like the devs wanted to take the easy way out in a few situations (Player being Sasha Cole, Xavier actually being a friend of HAL, the Ghost just escaping like nothing happened and being able to interfere with HALs scripts...) Overall, I adored this game.  I struggle with this next phrase because i don't fully mean it and understand why it is the way it is... but I'm glad I bought it on sale and not full price as it's not quite worth the full price.  I mostly say this due to game length and lack of choice in endings.  I took a look and it looks like this might be a first time game from this dev, who I'm guessing is solo or very small which is VERY exciting to see if this is their freshman showing.

Things I LOVED:
-Dynamic story telling.  There was a clear storyline running through from start to finish.  Not overly convoluted, not too cliche or simple.  Were the twists a little predictable?  Maybe a few.  But that didn't take away from the impact when they hit anyway.  The pacing of those drops were excellently done.
-Style was lovely.  I REALLY dug the overall look of the game.  The various tools you got to us, the puzzles you go to solve... all from a single terminal.  It made me think of a hacking game from the early 00s of gaming sites that I loved to play over and over.
-The voice acting was excellent.  Really stellar work.
-The game itself.  It's just really enjoyable.  It was well paced, the mystery was fun, the story was easy to follow, the puzzles were a bit easy but a few had some real challenges in there.  One puzzle was a bit too much of a lateral thinking puzzle, BUT that was one of the best twists of the whole game so I can overlook it. 

Things I wish were different (not bad, just things I wanted more of):
-it's far too short.  It took me about 4 hours to complete and that was going very slow and taking my time, looking at my phone a lot and doing a few other things at the same time. (thanks ADHD)  The story telling and plot that the game is driving could easily have been a full scale game.  And I'd pay good money for it, too.  This is top notch story telling from a new dev and I hope we see more.
-Lack of use of cool tools.  You're introduced to several cool mini puzzles throughout the game like a car analyzer, a bomb diffuser, and chemical component analyzer.  All of them have robust rules and options with them.  And they're all used only once.  You gave us so many cool toys.. let us play with them!!
-No story diversity with a [spoiler] really weak and bad ending [/spoiler].  While the story they have given is lovely, your choices don't matter.  There is just that ending.  I wanted more options, i wanted to affect the story with how i played and wanted the game reward cleverness (i.e. if you found a certain name on a certain list before you were told to.)

All that being said, if you like mystery games, if you like hack style games, this is a great choice.  I am very excited to see what this dev does in the future.  If this is their first showing, we are in for some real gems in the future!!

TL;DR: This game is a 3-hour long visual novel with not-that-meaningful choices, good music and sound effects, narration, and an interesting but short linear story line. 0 replay-ability.

The nice things:

[spoiler]1. The cutscenes where the game shows you that time has passed is nice. The subtle drug-taking noises and coughing noises makes a good addition. Even though there is no real graphics here, it shows that the developers put in a lot of efforts in making the game immersive.
2. The interface and UI, especially the keyboard noises you make when you are typing, makes me reminiscent of a time when I wasn't even alive. It just feels nice to type things and click on things.
3. Narration is good, not crazy impressive, but good. That's a hard bar to pass by my standards.
4. Mechanics are nice, problem solving feels rewarding, visual and audio clues are subtle yet noticeable.[/spoiler]

The first playthrough of the game is amazing, but there are a few nick-picking things.

[spoiler]1. Agents not reacting differently when you call them by their first names instead of their last names.
2. During the first interaction with HAL, I chose to report her to my supervisor. And after the second one, I ratted her out again because I felt even if she helped me she is still wanted for good reasons. Even when I ratted her out twice, she still choose to help me with mellow tones and such. I'd expect some type of pissed-off-but-still-have-to-work-with-you type of attitude. (This can be explained with later plots but, a pissed-off reaction would've been nice, it would feel like the game recognized my choices.)
3. During the agent Andrews infiltration event, the security camera added immersion but served little to no purpose. She could complete her task no matter what, and even though we spotted for her to avoid the walking personnel, it didn't seem to matter because the guy didn't do anything when he literally saw her in the first pass.
4. I just finished my second playthrough, this game has 0 replay-ability. Everything is the same, your choices don't matter where the story goes, Tanner will always die in the end. I guess its building for a potential sequal.
5. The game teased the true identity of the Mike waaaaaay too easy. As the head of the entire secret service unit, you would go ahead and call 'your friend' during work through secured line just chatting? Also, he lied about having a wife while his files show that he is single. Meanwhile the game constantly push how weird Skinner is but they exposed the lead on Mike way too early and way too easily.[/spoiler]

Finally, if you have finished the game.
[spoiler]Can anyone tell me what 25000100193555 means? This code is written in the ALICE file in your trashbin if you open the folder before HAL gives you the code. If you open it again after HAL gives you the code it updates to the usual letter from Alice. The code doesn't open any files in the HDD, I wonder what its used for, its the only remaining mystery in this game for me.[/spoiler]

review_text_raw:
TL;DR
Overall a solid, if short, experience. If you like games similar to Killer Frequency, Hypnospace Outlaw, or even Papers Please, you will enjoy this. I felt the story was paced well enough and presented well enough to keep my interest to the end. My only complaints are the length of the game, a lack of content, and I had the story fairly well figured out before the climax. The puzzles were well put together, for the most part, but none of them felt difficult and I completed them pretty quickly, and enjoyed doing so. For 15$ I think it's worth your time if you're looking for a few hours to kill doing detective work. On sale I definitely recommend it.

GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is pretty simplistic. As stated above similar to the likes of Hypnospace Outlaw where you navigate a computer system using different apps and given information (files) to solve puzzles. The puzzles themselves I felt weren't overly difficult, but done well enough to definitely have me pay more attention to various things. They also do a great job with handling a few very important plot points in the game. One section, in particular, did get me rather anxious. Overall it does its job well, and I enjoyed pretty much all of it. The only problem I had overall with gameplay was the lack of content. It gives you some interesting tools to utilize, then just sort of forgets about them.

SOUND:
I really enjoyed what they did with this game. The music really fit the moments and added some flair to various points in the game. The ambient sound and environmental sounds are also done VERY well to play parts in the game. It may not blow your mind, but I appreciate the amount of effort they put forth in this front. The soundtrack is quite good.

STORY:
They do a good job giving a good detective story to play out. You may or may not figure out the twists and turns it will take. Unfortunately I had some of the big reveals pegged within the first hour. On the other hand, I still enjoyed it enough to keep going. It won't blow your mind or take you into the depths of the universe they created; it gives you what it needs to, and executes it well. I don't care if a story blows my mind, so long as I have fun experiencing it, which I did here.

As a side note for the story, they did do a great job with a few moments of making them actually very tense. My only complaint, as stated above, is that it felt too short.


IN CONCLUSION:
The Operator is a solid entry into this detective-like puzzle-solving Operating System-simulator genre. I enjoyed my time with it, I do enjoy the mechanics of utilizing a computer in game to solve various puzzles with information that is available, but you have to search for. While sort, it didn't overstay its welcome and accomplished what it set out to do. I will greatly look forward to another game of this style if they decide to do one!

review_text_raw:
If you are looking for a good puzzle/detective guy in the chair game to scratch that itch made by an indie developer to entertain you for 3 hours with great gameplay, great puzzles that don't hold your hand and are satisfying to solve, great voice acting, introducing a couple of interesting game mechanics beyond "click face and search for name here" and a pretty good linear story, then this is the game for you. I bought it at 10% off and really enjoyed it, will definitely be on the look out for the next game this developer makes, and would recommend it to anyone with the expectation that its a good indie game.  

If you are looking for a deep, multi ending detective game where choices matter and there's endless replayability, this is not the game for you. I think the two critiques I see the most of is that fact the game is short and doesn't have multiple endings. For the length side, I think complaining that a game isn't long enough is a pretty good complaint to have. The game isn't perfect, but its entertaining and I hope the developer makes a longer game in the future using the success from this game to better utilize some of the interesting game mechanics that get introduced but then not used again (there's a few). 

Whether it's worth the price is subjective. The developer gave the reasoning that it's about the length of a movie, around the price of similar games, and so that's why it's at the price that it is. I don't know how much that justifies the price for this game, which I feel is a few dollars more expensive than similar games, but since I liked the demo, the movie comparison seemed reasonable enough for me (at least given some reason instead of no reason at all) and I wanted to support the developer, so I went for it when it first released. Overall, I am very satisfied with the game, had a good time, and would buy it again. 

Not having multiple endings doesn't bother me much. If the "choices" are scattered throughout the game, I'm not replaying, solving puzzles I already know the answers too, just to change a couple of dialogue options. The same thing for if the choice is at the end and there's no individual save feature for me to go back to. I think it's fair to expect an indie developer to just make a game that's fun to play once. There's dialogue options that don't really matter, but I found the characters you interact with the most really endearing and felt connected very quickly.

[h1]The Operator – Review[/h1]
I’ve just finished my first playthrough of [i]The Operator[/i], and it really got under my skin. At first, it feels like a clear throwback to [i]Orwell[/i] — digging through files, connecting clues, and sitting with that constant, uneasy sense of surveillance. The retro desktop setup is spot-on and makes the whole thing feel strangely real. About halfway through, I started wondering if the game itself was testing me. Was I part of the experiment? That thought stuck with me right to the end. The puzzles are clever and rewarding, and the story ramps up quickly, leaving you with plenty to think about. I’m already planning another run to see what I missed.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Holds It Back[/h2]
That said, the biggest drawback is its length. At around three to four hours, it ends just as you’re fully immersed. I couldn’t help but think how much more replayable it could be with a few extra systems layered on top.
[list]
[*]Randomised agents
[*]Modular or shuffled case fragments
[*]Overlapping investigative threads across multiple cases
[/list]
Something like that would fit perfectly with the game’s investigative tone and make it feel less like a one-and-done experience. Piecing together evidence that changes each run would add a lot of longevity.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Similar Games Worth Mentioning[/h2]
If you enjoyed [i]Orwell[/i] or [i]Her Story[/i], you’ll feel right at home here. That said, if you’re looking for longer playtime, there are other options worth considering:
[list]
[*][b]Orwell[/b] – branching choices across multiple episodes
[*][b]Return of the Obra Dinn[/b] – a sprawling mystery with dozens of characters
[*][b]The Case of the Golden Idol[/b] – interconnected cases with deep logic puzzles
[*][b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] – hacking and social engineering-driven investigations
[*][b]Shadows of Doubt[/b] – a procedural detective sandbox with near-infinite replayability
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
This is a short, sharp, and stylish thriller that absolutely nails its atmosphere and narrative hooks. It’s not perfect — some dialogue feels stiff, and the illusion of choice can occasionally be frustrating — but for a few hours of tense, thought‑provoking gameplay, it’s absolutely worth it. I just hope a possible sequel takes the next step and gives us the freedom to dig deeper, for longer.

Here's the bad news first: This game is maybe 3-4 hours long. The puzzles aren't too terribly hard to figure out and there doesn't seem to be any branching paths to the narrative. Also, the blur effect on the cutscenes could be irritating to some.

The good news: It's a well-told story that IS short, but it's surprisingly punchy. A few of the puzzles are gripping to solve and the story builds consistently with intrigue and suspense as you go. It's all organic and nothing feels out of place. The soundtrack is *superbly* done with music fitting pretty much everything you're doing. 

$14 for 3 hours is kind of a steep ask for a video game, but considering how much it is to go to a movie theater these days and spend more for *less*, your mileage may vary. Worth it on a sale, I'd wager.

Give this one a look! The ending definitely has some hints to a possible sequel and if they make one, I have faith they'll make an even longer game with more to do as this feels almost like a tech demo or a trial run. I want them to really sink in a longer story, more intrigue, more stuff to do, and give us the chance to find a better path than just one single narrative. 

Choice matters to the player and if we feel like nothing we did really changed anything on the main scenario, it can be jarring when the ending piledrives us with how things turned out despite our efforts. Food for thought, Bureau 81!

Anyways, I'm giving this a recommend. Your choice to wait for sale or not, but it's not so steep you won't enjoy yourself with a well-crafted and thought-out experience. Light on gaming, heavy on story and immersion.

An extremely solid game with fantastic voice acting, music, atmosphere, and cinematics. I'm particularly partial to the camera feeds which mask lower fidelity models (and occasionally wonky animation if you really look for it) through camera filters that made me guess multiple times if I was viewing real footage until I caught on to the trickery.

It has a controversial ending, especially due to the short length of the game. Personally I respected it, but it would've landed much better if there were more things to do. It lacks a lot of the exploration that you can do in a similar title, Hypnospace Outlaw. The game is broadly very linear, with a few choices and decisions that change things up, but you can't uncover hidden optional content like in HSO. The execution of being an operator ends up playing closer to Phoenix Wright (story over mechanics) than HSO. 

I very particularly remember feeling disappointed when I assumed control of [spoiler] HAL [/spoiler] and was hoping I could at least play a day (if not campaign) of that. Also the [spoiler] bomb defusal [/spoiler] mechanic was pretty fun. If they made it a side mode (non voiced of course, it only has one correct answer as of now) I'd probably play that for a good bit.

That said, I quite enjoyed it, and it's pretty unique. I hope they build upon this solid base in a future title, there's real potential for something I'd really fall in love with. Unfortunately, they delisted the demo (cringe) but if you liked the demo, it's like 20% of the game but you'd definitely like the game. If you're skeptical or broke, probably better to wait for a sale for ~$10.

Pleasantly surprised how good this game actually is. Good story and the gameplay is top notch. I hope there's more games like this in the future. 

You're Evan Tanner, a newly hired FDI phone operator. Your first day on the job is a simple case of "Who done it"? Pretty easy, since it's your first day. You have a couple "tools" at your disposal, make use of them. Answer some calls from your friend, AKA your supervisor and the main "BOSS", The Director. After your first day, you go home, feed the cat, microwave a dinner and watch a little TV. Time for bed so you can do it all tomorrow. Day 2. You get a call from a field agent about a missing person in New Mexico, the agent calling is sure she's full of :poop: so you do a little digging. This time you have a few more tools to learn. While examining the newly uploaded photos, your computer starts to act a little, "strange", YOU'VE BEEN HACKED. This is where the story really takes off and has plenty of twists and turns you won't know which way is straight. Now you have some pretty cool toys to play with, forensics (Mind you this game is set in 1992, so kinda limited) but you make due with what you have.  I'll leave it at this stopping point. It's a very fun and interesting game that will keep you on the edge of your seat and guessing, "Now WHAT"?!?!?! 

Have Fun, Agent Tanner...

Very well produced game. I enjoyed the aesthetic and the soundtrack. The story was engaging and kept me going for the 3 or so hours. Can't help but feel disappointed at the content on offer though. For 14 bucks? 3 hours is a bit of a stretch. 

-The game is much more hand-holdy than I anticipated. You click on pictures and then click on names for most of the game's tasks. There are a few solid logic puzzles. Maybe 2 or 3. The game is not difficult. There are 2 major set-pieces in the game. The first, concerning disarming a device, is very good. The second, concerning videos and maps, is a let down. It's mostly something you watch.

There seems to be some incentive to replay. There's also an ARG if you like that sort of thing. But for me the plot wasn't electric enough to engage outside of the fiction.

It's a very basic popcorn thriller. Not bad, but certainly milquetoast. There are 2 major twists. One can be seen from a mile away, the second is actually very clever but doesn't do much for the story other than shock you.

The game is well made. The story is engaging but pretty standard and cliche without any real themes to take away from it. The mystery gameplay is shallow and easy. Not a bad time to spend 3 hours though, so I'll end up recommending it.

review_text_raw:
The Good:

- The simulated computer UI is slick and responsive, and very immersive (so long if you suspend disbelief that technology was this advanced in the early 90s lol).
- The soundtrack perfectly sets the mood.
- Most of the connections between clues are interesting and fun to figure out.
- The story is engaging and well-paced.

The Bad:

- The game is too short! Most of my other points are variations of this complaint.
- Not enough cases/clues, so the central mystery builds extremely quickly.
- Some tools you use only once.
- The ending is rather abrupt and either downbeat or an annoying cliffhanger, depending on your perspective.
- Player choice is largely an illusion. Depending on choices, some events play out slightly differently and a tiny bit more of the backstory is revealed or not, but 95% of the story is identical, including the ending.
- Voice acting is fine, but not amazing
- All this feels like a hook for a (hopefully larger and longer) sequel

All in all though, the quality of what IS in the game plus its low price moves it to the recommend column for me. It is up to you if a game you can beat in a sitting or two is worth whatever price it is at the moment. For me, it was.

It's an ok game to kill a couple hours. I'm recommending, because I love that people make these kind of games, but I am a bit disappointed. It's VERY easy. The demo gave me Vigil Cases vibe, but turned out the game has incredibly strong and inescapable hand-holding. It's like Vigil Cases in tutorial mode. I thought I'd be looking through a bunch of databases and burrowing into various documents to find details that would solve cases. In reality I was mostly clicking on the dialogue, where NPCs would tell me exactly what to do, which usually involved no more than opening one file, looking up one name, or following a list of instructions.

There was a lot of lost potential here. Like, there's literally zero point in the terminal: the player never gets to figure out what command they should enter, it's always provided by the NPCs. There's no choice who to call, or what information to tell them, except in a couple places. I counted two cool puzzles that gave you an "Aha" moment, the rest was unfortunately easy and predictable.

In short, if you're looking for something to scratch the 'Golden Idol" or "Roottrees are Dead" itch, I wouldn't get your hopes up.

Very fun while it lasts: it's a interactive fiction where you are a intelligence agency operator trying to do your job by identifying crucial details with scripted in game calls. Not to spoil, but this involved entering key words into the correct prompt and linking information. 
Unfortunately, it only has one ending in a mostly linear path, so no matter what you do you'll pretty well get the same ending. 
but it's a fantastic short play. 
some highlights:
solve cases with database searches, evidence reviews, and crosslinking data for answers
A timed bomb defusal where you have to talk someone through not getting blown up
some espionage/live mission support for a *redacted* sting operation
some on the fly multiple choice dialogue making you second guess every option
a stellar ending. 

Sadly, it's less interactive and more fictional narrative than one would hope. 
Hopefully the sequel will have non-linear plots, side plots, and dynamic choices with more emphasis on your choices mattering and divergent paths. 

I highly recommend this to anyone who has an interest in puzzles and psedo-intelligencia government fiction/espionage thrills.

A 1990's-era X-Files-inspired game, you play as the titular Operator, one of many multi-talented personell tasked with assisting the agents of the Federal Department of Investigation (FDI), the fictional counterpart to the US FBI and, eventually, uncover a strange conspiracy.

The voice acting is excellent, really bringing life to all the characters. The puzzles are all logical and clever, especially if you keep track of prior cases.

The story is also excellent. It's only ~2 hours long, but it feels much longer than that, not because of padding, but because it manages to pack in a lot of meaningful intrigue and story beats in those 2 hours. It also has some excellent twists.

Would definitely recommend!

[spoiler]If you've played the game and found the ending lacking, good news: the end is not the end. All you need to continue the story is a web browser, a number found in a folder you can unlock earlier than normal with the right knowledge, and a key piece of information hidden in the Steam store page Metal Gear Style 1-style.[/spoiler]
